title: The badge, in Python
summary: Rewrite the week one name badge as real Python code on python.microbit.org instead of snapping blocks.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop again: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. This week you are not building a new badge. You are rebuilding the exact same badge from week one, except every block becomes a typed line of Python.

Ask: what did each block in your week one badge actually do? Before you open the editor, picture your old program block by block. `on start`, the `forever` block with a beating heart, and `on button A pressed` showing your own picture.

Imagine before you build: picture what each block looks like as a line of text instead of a puzzle shape.

1. A block you drag once becomes a line you type once.
2. A block that wraps other blocks, like `forever`, becomes a line ending in a colon.
3. Lines that were nested inside a block get typed indented underneath it instead.

Plan the order before you type: which line runs once at the start, and which lines are inside the loop that never ends. Note which lines only run when button A is pressed. Plan also means choosing one number of your own: how long the happy face should stay on screen after you press the button.

Five minutes on the same typing site you have been using. This week practice the exact shapes your code will use: a pair of quotation marks around a word, like "NAME", and a line that ends in a colon followed by an indented line underneath. Type a few practice lines that end in a colon, such as while True: typed out in full, then press Tab once and type the next line indented under it, then press Backspace or Shift+Tab to get back to the left edge before typing a line with no indent at all. Also practice typing a dot in the middle of a word with no space on either side, like display.show, since this week's code is full of names joined by dots.

figure.alt: A flow from top to bottom: import runs once, then scroll the name runs once, then a while True box contains show heart and sleep, show small heart and sleep, and the button A check, with a dashed green arrow looping from the bottom of that box back to its top, forever. A note warns that one missing colon or bad indent stops every line below it.

items.s: one typo here stops every line below it

steps.title: What the editor does with your text
steps.body:
The python.microbit.org editor does not send your actual words to the chip. When you click Send, or download a file and copy it over yourself, the editor turns the Python text you typed into a hex file, a single file that packs your whole program together with the exact pattern of instructions the chip's processor understands. That hex file, not your typed words, is what actually ends up stored on the micro:bit.

The chip does not see your program all at once the way you can look at the whole screen of code. It reads and runs one instruction at a time, starting at the top and working down, in the exact order you typed the lines. The while True: line is the only twist: once the chip reaches the bottom of that loop, it jumps back to the top of the loop and keeps running the same lines in order, again and again, forever.

That strict, in-order reading is exactly why a typo stops everything. A missing colon, a misspelled word, an indent one space too far in or out, and the editor cannot turn your text into a working hex file at all, or the chip gets confused partway through and stops making sense of the lines that follow. One small mistake anywhere in the file can keep every line after it, even lines that are perfectly correct on their own, from ever running.

steps.title: Type the badge in Python
steps.body:
Getting ready:

1. https://python.microbit.org is a website with a Python editor for the micro:bit.
2. Its `Send to micro:bit` button sends your code straight to the board over USB.
3. The first time, it may ask you to `Connect` the micro:bit before it can send.

Type the code:

1. Go to https://python.microbit.org and open the Python editor, not the block editor.
2. Delete any starter code.
3. Type `from microbit import *` on the first line. It brings in, or imports, every tool the micro:bit gives Python, like `display`, `Image` and `sleep`, so the rest of your code can use them.
4. Leave a blank line, then type `display.scroll("YOUR NAME")`, replacing YOUR NAME with your own name.
5. Type `while True:` on the next line.
6. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.HEART)`.
7. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(500)`, using the heartbeat pause you chose in week one instead of 500.
8. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.HEART_SMALL)`.
9. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(500)` again, using the same heartbeat pause, right after `HEART_SMALL`.
10. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `if button_a.was_pressed():`.
11. Make sure the line starts eight spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.HAPPY)`.
12. Make sure the line starts eight spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(1000)`.

Note: week one's loop had only one pause, right after the big heart, so the small heart flashed by with no pause before jumping back. This version pauses after both hearts equally, which is why it needs that second `sleep`. Delete that line after `HEART_SMALL` if you want to match week one exactly.

Compare it with week one:

1. `display.scroll(...)` before the loop is the same as `on start` scrolling your name once.
2. `while True:` is the same as the `forever` block, just written as text with a colon.
3. Each `display.show(...)` line is the same as a `show icon` block, naming the icon in parentheses.
4. Each `sleep(...)` line is the same as a `pause` block.
5. `if button_a.was_pressed():` is the same as `on button A pressed`, but it sits inside the loop.

Predict first: how long, in milliseconds, should the happy face stay on screen before the heartbeat picks back up? Change `sleep(1000)` to the number you choose.

Send it to the board:

1. Check that no line has a red wavy underline or a red dot beside its line number.
2. If your micro:bit is plugged in over USB, click `Send to micro:bit`.
3. If `Send to micro:bit` does not work in this browser, click `Save` and drag the `.hex` file onto the `MICROBIT` drive.

Make the heartbeat a function:

1. Put the cursor at the very start of the `display.scroll` line and press Enter twice, to make room above it.
2. On the first empty line, at the left edge, type `def beat():`.
3. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.HEART)`.
4. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(500)`, with your own heartbeat pause.
5. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.HEART_SMALL)`.
6. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(500)` again, with the same pause.
7. Inside `while True:`, delete the four heart and sleep lines.
8. In their place, on a line that starts four spaces in, type `beat()`.
9. On the next line, at the same indent, type `beat()` again.
10. Send it to the board: the heart now beats twice for every trip around the loop.

A function is a named piece of code you can use again. `def` means define: you teach Python a new word, `beat`, and the indented lines under it are what the word means. Typing `beat()` uses it; the parentheses say run it now. Four lines written once, used twice, and a change to the pause inside `beat` changes every beat at once.

Optional: swap `Image.HAPPY` for the picture you drew in week one. Write it as five rows of five digits from 0 to 9, separated by colons, like `Image("09090:99999:99999:09990:00900")`.

What you should see: your name scrolls once when the program starts, then the display beats between a big heart and a small heart forever, and pressing button A shows a happy face for the time you chose before the heartbeat picks back up again. No line has a red wavy underline before you send.

If it does not work:

1. The micro:bit scrolls an error message on its own LEDs the moment it starts: read the line number it names, go straight to that line in the editor, and check it for a missing colon or a wrong indent first.
2. Nothing happens at all: the code may not have reached the board; check no line has a red wavy underline, then click `Send to micro:bit` again.
3. The heart beats but button A does nothing: `if button_a.was_pressed():` needs to sit inside `while True:`, indented the same four spaces as the heartbeat lines above it, not outside the loop.
checklist: Name scrolls once when the program starts
Heart beats: big heart, pause, small heart, pause, on repeat, from a beat() function I defined and called twice
Button A shows a happy face for a length of time I chose myself, then goes back to the heartbeat
No red error message shows under the editor before you Send
I wrote down how long I chose for the happy face to show, and why

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
Typing Python for the micro:bit opens up new ways to make a mistake that blocks never allowed. Three show up constantly.

A missing colon: forgetting the colon at the end of a while or if line. Python needs that colon to know a new block of indented lines is about to start, and without it, the very next line confuses it.

A wrong indent: a line meant to run inside the while True: loop, or inside the if button_a.was_pressed(): check, typed back at the left edge instead of indented under it, or indented at the wrong level entirely. Python uses the indent itself to decide what is inside which block, so an indent in the wrong place changes what your program actually does, even if every word is spelled right.

When something is wrong, the micro:bit itself often tells you, scrolling an error message across its own LED grid the moment it starts up, something like line 5 SyntaxError or line 8 IndentationError. That scrolling message names the exact line the chip choked on and roughly what kind of mistake it found. Read the line number first, go straight to that line in the editor, and check it for a missing colon or a wrong indent before you check anything else.

Write one line in your bug diary for each error you hit today: what the scrolling message said, and what you changed to fix it. Also write down the number of milliseconds you chose for the happy face, and why you kept it or changed it from a full second.

steps.title: Good place to stop
steps.body:
Your Python badge is built and running: name scrolls, the heart beats, and button A shows a happy face, so this is a good end to week one of this quest; the rest is next week.

Before you stop:

1. In the editor, click `Save`, and keep the downloaded `.hex` file somewhere you will find it again. The editor also keeps your code in this browser, but only on this laptop, and clearing the browser loses it, so the saved file is your safe copy.
2. Unplug the micro:bit; the program you already sent stays on the chip either way.
3. Write in the Maker's Log one thing that surprised you about typing Python instead of snapping blocks.

Week two starts at the next step, Find the answer yourself, where you learn what to do when your own code breaks and nobody is there to ask.

When you come back, plug the micro:bit back in and reopen https://python.microbit.org. If your code is not already there, click `Open` and pick your saved file, or drag it onto the editor.

steps.title: Find the answer yourself

figure.alt: A mock of an error from python.microbit.org's serial area. The first line says Traceback, most recent call last. The next two lines say which lines were running: line 11, in module, then line 5, in beat. The last line, highlighted, gives the real error: NameError, name 'Sleep' isn't defined. Beside it, the micro:bit scrolls the same last line across its LEDs. A note says copy the exact words of the last line.

items.s: read the last line first, not the top
copy the exact words of the last line

steps.body:
Sooner or later your own code will break with nobody there to ask. Here is the order to try things in, and you practise it now on a bug you plant on purpose.

1. In `def beat():`, change the first `sleep` to `Sleep`, with a capital S.
2. Look at the editor before you send it: a line the editor already knows is wrong gets a red wavy underline and a red dot by its line number. Hover over the dot and read what it says.
3. Click `Send to micro:bit` anyway, and watch the board.
4. Read the last part of the message first, not the start. The micro:bit scrolls the line number and the error, like `line 5 NameError name 'Sleep' isn't defined`, and if you run it in the simulator, the full message shows in the serial area under the simulated board. The last line names the real problem; the lines above it only say which lines were running when it broke.
5. Copy the exact words of that last line into your Maker's Log, not a rough memory of them. `IndentationError: unexpected indent` and `NameError: name 'Sleep' isn't defined` point to two completely different mistakes.
6. Look it up in the official reference: open the `Reference` tab on the left of the editor, find the part your broken line uses, here `sleep`, and compare your line with its example, letter for letter.
7. Make the smallest change that could fix it, one change at a time, and send it again before you change anything else.
8. Only if it is still broken after all that, ask Ask. Give it the four things from How to ask AI a good question back in week 5, and paste the exact error words.
9. If Ask's answer does not fix it either, show a grown-up what you have tried so far.

What you should see: after step 3 the board scrolls the error instead of beating the heart; after step 7 the heart beats again, and you did not need Ask or a grown-up for this one.

If it does not work:

1. No red underline, no error, and the heart still beats: the capital S did not stick, or you changed a different line; check the first `sleep` line inside `def beat():`.
2. The scroll is too fast to read: press the reset button on the back of the micro:bit to run it again from the start, or run it in the simulator and read the serial area.
3. Ask answers with a question instead of explaining: it is missing one of the four things; answer whichever one it asks for.

You are done when: your planted bug is fixed by the reference, not by Ask, and you can say out loud which rung fixed it. The next real bug of your own gets the same ladder.

steps.title: Your turn: button B
steps.body:
The one-line spec: pressing button B shows a different picture than button A's happy face, for a length of time you choose.

You already have everything this needs: `if button_a.was_pressed():` as your model, `button_b`, and `Image.SAD` or any image you like. Give it a real, focused 15 minutes.

If you want the guide instead: `Button B shows a different picture`, below in this quest's extras, walks through each line.

You are done when: pressing button B shows your own picture on the micro:bit, separately from button A's happy face, and you can say which line you copied from button A's check and which one you changed.
checklist: Pressing button B shows a picture different from button A's happy face
The button B check sits at the same indent as the button A check, inside while True:
I chose my own length of time for the picture to show, and wrote down why
I named, out loud or in the log, which line I copied and which one I changed

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the badge running, and the Python code you typed, copied out or screenshotted.

extras.title: Button B shows a different picture
extras.body:
This is the step-by-step version of Your turn: button B. Use it if 15 minutes were not enough on your own.

1. Open your project at https://python.microbit.org.
2. Keep the code you already wrote, from `from microbit import *` down to the button A check.
3. Make sure the line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `if button_b.was_pressed():`, lined up under the button A check, not inside it.
4. Make sure the line starts eight spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.show(Image.SAD)`.
5. Make sure the line starts eight spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `sleep(1000)`, or a number you choose yourself.
6. Check that no line has a red wavy underline, then click `Send to micro:bit`.

What to notice: both button checks sit at the same indent level, directly inside `while True:`.

figure.alt: A micro:bit screen showing a sad face: two eyes, and a mouth with corners higher than the middle.

spec.caption: A sad face for button B, mouth corners higher than the middle, the opposite curve from a happy face.

extras.title: Change the message when you shake it
extras.body:
Make a message appear only when you shake the badge.

1. Open your project at https://python.microbit.org.
2. Inside `while True:`, right after your two `beat()` lines, on a line that starts four spaces in, type `if accelerometer.was_gesture("shake"):`.
3. Make sure the line starts eight spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `display.scroll("SHAKEN")`, or a word you choose yourself.
4. Check that no line has a red wavy underline, then click `Send to micro:bit`.

What to notice: `was_gesture` reports true only once per shake, so it will not repeat until you shake again.

extras.title: Design your own Python badge feature
extras.body:
What is one thing you wish your Python badge could do that it cannot yet?

Design one new feature for the badge and type it yourself.

It must use `while True:` and at least one `if` you write yourself.
It must have one number you choose by testing, like a pause or a threshold.
It must be shown running on the real micro:bit to someone in your house.

Sketch it on paper before you type.

How to know it works: someone who has never seen your code can describe what it does after watching.

extras.title: Ask the accelerometer again, in Python
extras.body:
Find out what the accelerometer really reads when nothing is moving it at all, in Python this time.

1. Predict first: guess the number `accelerometer.get_z()` will show while your micro:bit lies flat and still on the table, screen up. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Open python.microbit.org and add `display.scroll(accelerometer.get_z())` as its own line inside your `while True:` loop, four spaces in.
3. Send the program and read the number while the micro:bit lies flat and still on the table.
4. Flip the micro:bit over, screen down, still and flat, and read the number again.
5. Write down both numbers and compare them to your week 2 numbers if you still have them.

Compare: was your screen-up number close to zero, as most people guess, or close to 1024? What changed when you flipped it?

The chip is not broken and nothing is shaking it; it is feeling the steady pull of gravity, the same 1024 milli-g in a different direction depending on which way up it lies.

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why a sensor that is not moving at all still answers with a big number instead of zero.
